name: Circle formation

derived_from.relation: A circle is a family of patterns; forming some circle is easier than forming a given pattern, and it is the precursor of uniform circle formation [Feletti2024Optimal].

summary: Robots must reach positions on a common circle.
statement: $n$ robots start at distinct points and must reach a configuration in which all of them lie on one circle, at distinct points, and stay there. Uniform circle formation additionally asks for a regular $n$-gon.

primer.intro: Think of dancers who must spread out on one common circle, each at a different spot on it, without anyone drawing the circle first. There are $n$ **robots**, points at distinct places in the plane; their positions form the **configuration**. Each robot repeats a **Look–Compute–Move cycle**: it takes a **snapshot** of where the other robots are (Look), decides on a destination point (Compute) and moves towards it (Move). They are identical, silent, **oblivious** (no memory between cycles), and each uses its own **local coordinate system** (origin, axes, unit of length and handedness). A **scheduler** (an adversary) decides the **activation** of robots, that is, when each performs a cycle; in the basic version it is ASYNC, so each phase may take any finite time, and every move is a **non-rigid move**: the adversary may stop a robot after it has travelled some minimum distance $\delta$. The robots must reach a configuration in which all of them lie on one circle, at distinct points (not necessarily evenly spaced), and stay there.

ideas.title: Use the smallest enclosing circle and walk out to it
ideas.idea:
1. Every robot computes the **smallest enclosing circle** (SEC) of all robots. It is unique and does not depend on any local coordinate system, so all robots compute the same circle.
2. A robot already on the circle stays where it is.
3. A robot inside the circle moves straight outwards, along the ray from the centre through itself, to the circle.
4. A robot exactly at the centre has no ray; it first steps a little away from the centre.
5. If several robots lie on the same ray, only the outermost one moves out; the others first step sideways onto free rays, so that no two robots ever land on the same point.
ideas.analysis: Robots that move from inside onto the circle never change the smallest enclosing circle, so the circle stays fixed while robots move at different speeds and act on outdated snapshots. Each robot inside needs only finitely many moves, since each move covers at least $\delta$ or reaches the circle. This is the first phase of the uniform circle algorithm of Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Viglietta, which forms even a regular $n$-gon (hence a circle) in ASYNC without **chirality** (agreement on the clockwise direction) [Flocchini2017Uniform], the catalogue's current best. Steps 4 and 5 are simplified here; the paper handles robots at the centre and robots on a common ray as separate cases.
ideas.why_it_matters: The smallest enclosing circle is the standard common reference for disoriented robots, reused in pattern formation, gathering and leader election.

ideas.title: Move only inside your own zone, then slide along the circle
ideas.idea:
1. Compute the smallest enclosing circle and use its centre as the origin of polar coordinates.
2. A robot at the centre steps off it, by less than the distance of any other robot from the centre.
3. Otherwise, find your two neighbours in angular order around the centre and draw the rays halfway (by angle) to each of them. The region between these two rays is your **exclusive zone** for this cycle: no other robot will move into it.
4. A robot inside the circle moves outwards within its zone towards the circle; a robot on the circle slides along it towards the angle halfway between its neighbours, without ever leaving an empty arc larger than a half circle (which would shrink the circle).
ideas.analysis: Exclusive zones guarantee that two robots never end up at the same point. That matters: two robots on one point get the same snapshot, so a scheduler that always activates them together, with suitable local coordinate systems, can keep them together forever. Défago and Souissi show that in SSYNC the robots reach the circle and then converge towards even spacing without necessarily reaching it [Defago2008NonUniform]; reaching exactly even spacing needed later work (see uniform circle formation).
ideas.why_it_matters: It introduced the exclusive-zone trick for avoiding inseparable robots and the "slide towards the middle of your neighbours" rule for even spacing.

glossary.definition: a computing entity modelled as a point of the plane (a unit disc for fat robots); all robots run the same algorithm
the positions of all $n$ robots at one instant, a multiset of points of the plane

one activation of a robot: in Look it takes a snapshot, in Compute it determines a destination point from that snapshot alone (and its own light, where lights exist), in Move it travels towards that point
the configuration as a robot observes it in Look (with the colours of the lights it sees, where lights exist), expressed in its local coordinate system
a robot keeps no memory from one Look–Compute–Move cycle to the next: Compute uses only the current snapshot

the origin, axes, unit of length and handedness in which a robot expresses its snapshot and its destination; robots agree on none of these unless the setting assumes chirality, one common axis or a common compass

the adversary that decides when each robot is activated: FSYNC activates every robot in every round, SSYNC a nonempty subset of the robots in each round, the sequential scheduler exactly one robot per round, and ASYNC lets each phase of each cycle take any finite time; every robot is activated infinitely often
the scheduler's choice to let a robot perform one Look–Compute–Move cycle; a robot that is not activated stays still
a move that the adversary may stop before the destination, but only after the robot has travelled at least the distance $\delta$
the unique smallest circle that contains a given finite set of points (by default the robots of the configuration), abbreviated SEC; it does not depend on any local coordinate system
agreement of all robots on the clockwise direction (handedness) of their local coordinate systems, with no agreement on axes, unit or origin

for one cycle of a robot $r$, the wedge between the two rays from the centre of the smallest enclosing circle that bisect the angles between $r$ and its two angular neighbours; no other robot moves into it during that cycle

history: Circle formation was first proposed as a way to reach a uniform circle by oblivious robots without a common orientation [Defago2002Circle]; the first algorithms formed a circle and only converged towards uniformity [Defago2008NonUniform]. The question was **whether disoriented, oblivious robots can form a circle at all**, under which scheduler.

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or epochs (ASYNC) until the task is done; "finite" when only solvability is known

measures.name: Colours
measures.description: colours of the light per robot (0 for oblivious robots)

variants.title: Circle formation
variants.summary: Robots must place themselves on a common circle, not necessarily evenly spaced; solved in ASYNC without chirality through uniform circle formation.

results.note: Introductory for ASYNC and current best: Theorem 6.1 forms a uniform circle, hence a circle, in ASYNC without chirality and with non-rigid moves.

variants.notes: The first circle formation papers are semi-synchronous; see the SSYNC setting. Checked against the full text of [Flocchini2017Uniform].

variants.title: Circle formation, SSYNC
variants.summary: In SSYNC the first algorithms formed a circle and then converged towards a uniform one.

results.note: No chirality needed; proofs only sketched (as stated by [Defago2008NonUniform]).

assumes: a maximum step length per robot instead of adversarial non-rigid moves
results.note: Forms a circle and converges towards a uniform one without reaching it.

variants.notes: Défago and Souissi call their robots disoriented although they assume chirality; Flocchini et al. use disoriented to exclude chirality. Checked against the full text of [Defago2008NonUniform]; [Defago2002Circle] was not reachable.

figure.caption: Circle formation: robots at distinct points must place themselves at distinct points of one common circle and stay there; the spacing need not be uniform [Defago2002Circle]. Shown: the first phase of [Flocchini2017Uniform] in SSYNC rounds: every robot computes the smallest enclosing circle (dashed), which never changes; a ringed (activated) robot inside moves out along the ray from the centre, possibly stopping early; the robot at the centre first steps off it.
